plain_english: Remember: it's not just wanting power and wealth that makes you dependent on others. Even wanting peace, free time, travel, or education can do the same thing. Here's the truth: whatever outside thing you value highly will put you under someone else's control. So what's the difference between wanting to be a senator and not wanting to be one? What's the difference between craving power and being happy with ordinary life? What's the difference between saying "I'm miserable because I have nothing to do except sit with my books like a corpse" and saying "I'm miserable because I have no time to read"?
original_excerpt: Remember that not only the desire of power and of riches makes us mean and subject to others, but even the desire of tranquillity, and of leisure, and of travelling abroad, and of learning. For, to speak plainly, whatever the external thing may be, the value which we set upon it places us in subjection to others. What then is the difference between desiring to be a senator or not desiring to be one; what is the difference between desiring power or being content with a private station; what is the difference between saying, I am unhappy, I have nothing to do, but I am bound to my books as a corpse; or saying, I am unhappy, I have no leisure for reading?
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity

plain_english: Greetings and power are external things that aren't up to you. So is a book. Why do you choose to read? Tell me. If you're just reading to be entertained or to learn some facts, you're foolish and can't handle real work. But if you're reading for the right reason, what else could that be except a calm and happy life? If reading doesn't give you a calm and happy life, what's the point?
original_excerpt: For as salutations and power are things external and independent of the will, so is a book. For what purpose do you choose to read? Tell me. For if you only direct your purpose to being amused or learning something, you are a silly fellow and incapable of enduring labor. But if you refer reading to the proper end, what else is this than a tranquil and happy life ([Greek: eusoia])? But if reading does not secure for you a happy and tranquil life, what is the use of it?
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity

plain_english: But it does give me security, the man says, and that's why I'm upset that I'm losing it. What kind of peaceful, happy life is this that anyone can mess up? Not just Caesar or his friends, but a crow, a flute player, a fever, or any of thirty thousand other things? A truly peaceful and happy life has nothing more reliable than staying steady and being free from obstacles. Now I'm called to do something. I'll go with the goal of following the right rules. I'll act with humility and steadiness. I won't desperately want or hate external things. Then I can pay attention to people — what they say and how they act. But not with bad intentions, and not so I can find fault or make fun of them. Instead, I turn to myself and ask: Do I make the same mistakes? How can I stop making them? I used to act badly too, but now I don't. Thank God.
original_excerpt: But it does secure this, the man replies, and for this reason I am vexed that I am deprived of it.—And what is this tranquil and happy life, which any man can impede, I do not say Cæsar or Cæsar's friend, but a crow, a piper, a fever, and thirty thousand other things? But a tranquil and happy life contains nothing so sure as continuity and freedom from obstacle. Now I am called to do something: I will go then with the purpose of observing the measures (rules) which I must keep, of acting with modesty, steadiness, without desire and aversion to things external; and then that I may attend to men, what they say, how they are moved; and this not with any bad disposition, or that I may have something to blame or to ridicule; but I turn to myself, and ask if I also commit the same faults. How then shall I cease to commit them? Formerly I also acted wrong, but now I do not: thanks to God.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity

plain_english: So why does this happen? Because we never read or write with the right goal in mind. We don't study so we can handle life's situations naturally and wisely. Instead, we just want to learn what the books say. We want to explain ideas to others. We want to solve logical puzzles and work through arguments. That's where we put our effort, so that's where we hit roadblocks. Do you insist on wanting things outside your control? Then expect to be blocked, frustrated, and disappointed.
original_excerpt: What then is the reason of this? The reason is that we have never read for this purpose, we have never written for this purpose, so that we may in our actions use in a way conformable to nature the appearances presented to us; but we terminate in this, in learning what is said, and in being able to expound it to another, in resolving a syllogism, and in handling the hypothetical syllogism. For this reason where our study (purpose) is, there alone is the impediment. Would you have by all means the things which are not in your power? Be prevented then, be hindered, fail in your purpose.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity

plain_english: But what if we read about action not just to see what's written about action, but to actually act well? What if we read about desire and avoiding things so we can get what we want and avoid what we don't want? What if we read about duty so we remember how things relate to each other and never act irrationally or against those relationships? Then we wouldn't get upset when something interrupts our reading. We'd be satisfied with doing the right actions that match what we've learned.
original_excerpt: But if we read what is written about action (efforts, [Greek: hormae]), not that we may see what is said about action, but that we may act well; if we read what is said about desire and aversion (avoiding things), in order that we may neither fail in our desires, nor fall into that which we try to avoid; if we read what is said about duty (officium), in order that remembering the relations (of things to one another) we may do nothing irrationally nor contrary to these relations; we should not be vexed, in being hindered as to our readings, but we should be satisfied with doing the acts which are conformable (to the
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity

plain_english: We shouldn't keep track of what we usually count: 'Today I read this many lines, I wrote this much.' Instead we should say: 'Today I acted the way philosophers teach. I didn't desire things I can't control. I only avoided things that are actually up to me. I wasn't afraid of that person. I didn't give in when someone begged me to do something wrong. I practiced patience, self-control, and cooperation with others.' That's what we should thank God for.
original_excerpt: relations), and we should be reckoning not what so far we have been accustomed to reckon: To-day I have read so many verses, I have written so many; but (we should say), To-day I have employed my action as it is taught by the philosophers; I have not employed my desire; I have used avoidance ([Greek: echchlisei]) only with respect to things which are within the power of my will; I have not been afraid of such a person, I have not been prevailed upon by the entreaties of another; I have exercised my patience, my abstinence, my co-operation with others; and so we should thank God for what we ought to thank him.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity

plain_english: There's only one path to happiness. Keep this rule ready morning, noon, and night: don't focus on things outside your control. Think that nothing truly belongs to you. Give everything up to God, to Fortune — let them manage what Zeus has put them in charge of. You should only pay attention to what's actually yours, what can't be taken from you. When you read, connect it back to this principle. Same with your writing and listening. This is why I can't call someone hardworking just because they read and write. Even if someone reads all night, I won't call them diligent if they don't know how their reading connects to what really matters.
original_excerpt: There is only one way to happiness, and let this rule be ready both in the morning and during the day and by night: the rule is not to look towards things which are out of the power of our will, to think that nothing is our own, to give up all things to the Divinity, to Fortune; to make them the superintendents of these things, whom Zeus also has made so; for a man to observe that only which is his own, that which cannot be hindered; and when we read, to refer our reading to this only, and our writing and our listening. For this reason I cannot call the man industrious, if I hear this only, that he reads and writes; and even if a man adds that he reads all night, I cannot say so, if he knows not to what he should refer his reading.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity

plain_english: You wouldn't call a man hardworking just because he stays up all night for a girl. Neither would I. But if he reads and writes for fame, I call him fame-seeking. If he does it for money, I call him money-loving, not hardworking. If he does it because he loves learning, I call him a learner. But if he works to keep his mind in its natural state and live according to that — only then do I call him truly hardworking.
original_excerpt: For neither do you say that a man is industrious if he keeps awake for a girl, nor do I. But if he does it (reads and writes) for reputation, I say that he is a lover of reputation. And if he does it for money, I say that he is a lover of money, not a lover of labor; and if he does it through love of learning, I say that he is a lover of learning. But if he refers his labor to his own ruling power that he may keep it in a state conformable to nature and pass his life in that state, then only do I say that he is industrious.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity

plain_english: Don't praise someone for things that everyone has in common. Praise them for their principles — these belong to each person and make their actions good or bad. Remember these rules. Be happy with what you have right now. Be satisfied with what comes when it's supposed to come. If you see something you've learned being put to use in your life, be delighted by it.
original_excerpt: For never commend a man on account of these things which are common to all, but on account of his opinions (principles); for these are the things which belong to each man, which make his actions bad or good. Remembering these rules, rejoice in that which is present, and be content with the things which come in season. If you see anything which you have learned and inquired about occurring to you in your course of life (or opportunely applied by you to the acts of life), be delighted at it.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity

plain_english: Have you gotten rid of bad attitudes and the habit of insulting people? Have you worked on rash anger, foul language, impatience, and laziness? If things that used to upset you don't bother you anymore — or at least not in the same way — then you can celebrate every single day. Today because you acted well in one situation. Tomorrow because you handled another situation well. This is a much better reason to celebrate than getting elected to high office or being made governor of a province. These improvements come from you and from the gods. Remember this: who gives you these gifts, who receives them, and why. If you keep these thoughts close to your heart, does it really matter where you are when you're happy? Does location matter when you're pleasing God? The gods are equally distant from every place. They see what's happening just as clearly no matter where you are.
original_excerpt: If you have laid aside or have lessened bad disposition and a habit of reviling; if you have done so with rash temper, obscene words, hastiness, sluggishness; if you are not moved by what you formerly were, and not in the same way as you once were, you can celebrate a festival daily, to-day because you have behaved well in one act, and to-morrow because you have behaved well in another. How much greater is this a reason for making sacrifices than a consulship or the government of a province? These things come to you from yourself and from the gods. Remember this, who gives these things and to whom, and for what purpose. If you cherish yourself in these thoughts, do you still think that it makes any difference where you shall be happy, where you shall please God? Are not the gods equally distant from all places? Do they not see from all places alike that which is going on?
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity
